facts.t: Forming a trade union was once a criminal conspiracy
facts.d: In 1921 a Madras court fined B. P. Wadia and fellow organisers £2,000 for the conspiracy of forming a union. Five years later the Trade Unions Act, 1926 legalised the very act — and the Constitution turned it into a fundamental right.

The Codes on Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security and Occupational Safety consolidated 29 central labour laws, including the 1926 Act. They were brought into force in November 2025 — but labour is on the Concurrent List, so a worker's actual protection depends on whether their state has notified rules.

facts.t: Gig workers entered the statute book by the side door
facts.d: The Social Security Code names gig and platform workers for the first time and requires aggregators to contribute 1–2% of turnover. The Industrial Relations Code does not mention them at all — so they gained a welfare fund without gaining a bargaining forum.

bank.q: The right to strike in India is best described as:
o: A statutory entitlement, not a fundamental right
A common-law right enforceable in civil courts
A right available only to government employees
bank.e: B. R. Singh (1989) called the strike an important weapon of trade unions without elevating it to a fundamental right, and T.K. Rangarajan (2003) held that government employees have neither a fundamental nor a statutory right to strike.

bank.q: With reference to Article 19(1)(c), consider the following statements:
s: It guarantees the right to form associations and unions.
It guarantees that every object of an association may be pursued.
It includes the right to associate only with those voluntarily admitted.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. All India Bank Employees' Association (1962) held that the right to form a union does not guarantee the fulfilment of every union objective, such as compulsory recognition.

bank.q: Match List I (case) with List II (holding):
pairs: A. State of Madras v. V.G. Row
1. Compulsory alteration of a voluntary association's composition is unconstitutional
2. Reasonableness under Article 19(4) must be tested objectively by courts
3. No fundamental or statutory right to strike for government employees
4. Restrictions on armed-forces-attached civilian staff upheld under Article 33
bank.e: V. G. Row set the objective reasonableness test; Damyanti Naranga protected voluntary composition; Achudan Nair applied the Article 33 carve-out; Rangarajan denied the right to strike.

bank.q: Which one of the following is NOT a worker-strengthening feature of the new Labour Codes?
o: Sole Negotiating Union threshold lowered to 30% membership by secret ballot
Gig and platform workers named in statute for the first time
Retrenchment threshold raised from 100 to 300 workers
Mandatory Grievance Redressal Committees regardless of union presence
bank.e: Raising the threshold to 300 lets most mid-sized factories retrench or close without prior government permission — it is listed among the changes that weaken protection.

bank.as: Article 19(1)(c) was never meant to be self-executing.
bank.rs: Collective bargaining, striking and picketing exist only as statutory creations that an ordinary majority can narrow.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion. The constitutional right to unionise carries no co-extensive constitutional right to be bargained with, which is why statutory maintenance matters so much.

bank.q: Consider the following statements about the Industrial Relations Code:
s: It subsumes the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
It requires 60 days' notice before a strike and bars strikes during conciliation or tribunal proceedings.
It explicitly recognises gig and platform workers.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Gig and platform workers appear in the Social Security Code, not the Industrial Relations Code — so they get contributions but no collective bargaining forum.

bank.q: Aggregator contributions to the Social Security Fund for gig and platform workers are set at:
o: A flat annual fee per worker
bank.e: 1–2% of turnover, with Aadhaar-linked worker registration. It is the first statutory recognition of the platform workforce.

bank.q: Arrange the following in correct chronological order:
items: Four Labour Codes brought into force
bank.e: Madras Labour Union (1918) → Trade Unions Act (1926) → T.K. Rangarajan (2003) → the four Labour Codes brought into force (November 2025).

bank.q: All of the following are cited as issues with India's labour framework EXCEPT:
o: Colonial continuities echoing the Public Safety Bill and Trade Disputes Act
Decriminalisation of compliance failures weakening deterrence
Uniform national minimum wages removing state-level variation
Federal unevenness because labour sits on the Concurrent List
bank.e: There is no uniform minimum wage under the notified rules — state-wise fluctuation persists, and that is itself listed as a concern.

bank.q: Which state was the first to enact a dedicated gig workers' law, ahead of Karnataka and Telangana?
bank.e: Rajasthan legislated in 2023, followed by Karnataka in 2025 and the Telangana Bill of 2025 drafted with the Telangana Gig and Platform Workers Union.

bank.q: With reference to the IFAT petition of 2021, consider the following statements:
s: It argued that classifying gig workers as partners rather than employees violates Articles 14, 21 and 23.
It was filed by the Indian Federation of App-based Transport Workers.
It sought the repeal of the Trade Unions Act, 1926.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The petition sought recognition as employees and access to social security, not repeal of the 1926 Act.

bank.as: Ratifying ILO Conventions 87 and 98 is proposed as a way forward.
bank.rs: Those Conventions concern freedom of association and the right to organise and bargain collectively.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — they address precisely the gap between India's guaranteed right to unionise and its unguaranteed right to be bargained with.
